opus-5.5.text:
I think both matter, but they play different roles at different stages.

When a model does something you didn't expect, the first instinct is usually to form a story. "Oh, it's probably the data mixture," or "it must be the learning rate schedule." That kind of intuition is valuable. In a system this large you can't check everything, so belief is what tells you where to look first. Without some prior, you'd just be wandering around.

The danger is that belief also makes you stop looking too early. You find something consistent with your story, you feel good, and you move on. But in large-scale training many different causes produce very similar symptoms. A loss spike, a capability regression, some weird behavior in evaluation: there are often five plausible explanations, and the one you already believed in isn't necessarily the right one.

So my view is that belief should decide the order of the search, and method should decide the conclusion. Concretely, that means a few things.

First, reproduce it. If you can't reliably reproduce the behavior, you're mostly debugging noise. A surprising number of "bugs" disappear once you rerun with a different seed.

Second, make the problem smaller. Find the smallest setting where it still happens: a smaller model, fewer steps, a subset of the data. Every time you shrink it, the space of explanations shrinks too.

Third, change one thing at a time and write down what you expected before you look at the result. That last part is important. If you don't commit to a prediction in advance, it's very easy to read whatever comes out as confirmation.

Fourth, actively try to kill your own hypothesis. Ask what you'd see if you were wrong, and go look for exactly that.

There's also a more emotional side. When you've spent days on something, you really want your explanation to be correct, partly because it would mean the time wasn't wasted. Being systematic protects you from yourself a bit. It's less exciting than having a flash of insight, but over time the people I find most reliable at this are the ones who have strong intuitions and are also very willing to be told by the experiment that they were wrong.

So I wouldn't frame it as belief versus method. Belief is the engine and method is the brake. You need both, and the skill is knowing when to rely on which.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the two aren't really opposites, and in practice you need both, but they operate on different timescales.

Belief is what keeps you going before you have any evidence. When a model does something weird, say it suddenly collapses on a benchmark it was doing fine on, or an agent starts looping on the same action, you often have no idea why. There are dozens of plausible causes. If you don't have some underlying conviction that the behavior is explainable, that there's a mechanism somewhere, it's very tempting to just shrug and say "models are stochastic" and move on. I've seen a lot of people do that. Belief in this sense is almost a stubbornness: I believe this is not noise, I believe there's a reason, and I'm going to find it.

But belief alone is dangerous, because it's exactly what makes you fall in love with your first hypothesis. You think "oh, it's the prompt format," and then you spend three days changing prompts when the actual problem is a tokenization bug or a data leak. So the systematic method is what protects you from your own belief. Change one thing at a time. Write down what you expect before you run the experiment, so you can't retroactively explain whatever happens. Build the smallest reproduction you can, because a bug you can trigger in ten lines is a bug you'll fix in an hour, and a bug that only shows up in the full pipeline can take weeks.

The way I'd put it is that belief sets the direction and the method sets the pace. Early on, belief dominates: you need the intuition to even know where to look. Later, the method should dominate, and the honest signal is whether you're willing to let an experiment kill a hypothesis you liked. If you never update, your "belief" is really just attachment.

One more thing I'd say is that with language models specifically, systematic debugging matters more than people expect, because our intuitions are often wrong. We anthropomorphize. We assume the model "understands" something or "forgot" something, and that framing can lead you away from the actual cause, which is usually something very mundane: a shift in the data distribution, a tool returning a slightly different format, an off-by-one in how context is truncated. So I try to hold my beliefs about why the model does something very loosely, and hold the discipline of the process much more tightly.

astra-6.text:
I think belief is useful for deciding whether to keep working, but it shouldn’t determine your explanation of what’s happening. You can believe there’s something interesting to discover, or that a problem is solvable. But when a model behaves unexpectedly, that belief is only a starting point.

The next step is to make the surprise concrete. What did you expect, what did you observe, and can you reproduce the difference? Then you can form a few hypotheses and design experiments that distinguish them. Maybe the model lacks a capability; maybe the prompt is ambiguous; maybe the evaluation is measuring something different from what you intended. Those explanations imply different next steps.

The tricky thing is that it’s very easy to invent a convincing story about a model’s behavior after seeing one example. So I want a working method that can tell me my story is wrong. Belief gives you patience to continue investigating; a systematic method helps that patience produce knowledge.

r001.rationale: The response recommends experiments to distinguish hypotheses about unexpected model behavior, but it does not identify ablation experiments for testing causes of pretraining behavior that differs from predictions at a given scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think belief is useful for deciding whether a problem is worth pursuing, but once you start debugging, you need a systematic method. You can believe that the model should be capable of something, but that belief doesn’t explain why it failed on a particular example.

So I would start with the concrete failure: What did the model see? What did it produce? Can we reproduce it? Then form a hypothesis and change one thing at a time. Maybe the instruction is ambiguous, maybe the model is missing information, or maybe our expectation is wrong. The point is to make those possibilities distinguishable through experiments.

Belief gives you the patience to keep investigating. But you also need to be willing to abandon your favorite explanation. Otherwise, it’s very easy to keep changing prompts until you get one successful result and convince yourself you’ve solved the problem.
